title: Planning Pipelines: Sources, Sinks, Networking and Encryption

concepts.heading: Choose the Smallest Pipeline That Meets the Requirement
concepts.body: Planning a pipeline starts from the source, the sink and what must happen in between. If the data only has to move, the least machinery wins. Pub/Sub has three subscription families. Pull and push subscriptions hand messages to a subscriber you run, while export subscriptions make the Pub/Sub service itself write each message to BigQuery or Cloud Storage. A fleet of delivery vans publishing JSON telemetry that must reach a BigQuery table within seconds, with no filtering or enrichment, fits a BigQuery subscription: nothing to deploy, scale or monitor. Add a transform, a join or an aggregation and a subscriber is needed, which is where a streaming Dataflow job earns its place. Between pull and push, pull suits very high volume and private workers because the client controls the delivery rate, while push needs a public HTTPS endpoint and delivers one message per request, so it fits webhooks and Cloud Run. A Dataproc cluster for a pass-through load is the heaviest option and rarely the answer.

concepts.heading: Contracts and Change Data Capture at the Edges
concepts.body: Pipelines break at the boundaries, so plan the contract and the buffer. A Pub/Sub schema, in Apache Avro or Protocol Buffer format and attached to a topic, enforces the format of the message data: a message that does not conform is not published. When four product teams share one topic and subscribers keep failing on missing or misnamed fields, the schema stops bad data at the source for every consumer. For database sources, Datastream captures change data from databases such as PostgreSQL and can write the change events to Cloud Storage. Dataflow templates can then read those files and load BigQuery, Spanner or Cloud SQL. Landing changes in Cloud Storage first gives a durable, replayable record. Know the limits of the neighbours: Database Migration Service targets Cloud SQL and AlloyDB for PostgreSQL, and BigQuery Data Transfer Service loads into BigQuery, so neither writes to Spanner.

concepts.heading: Networking: Keep Workers Private and Inside the Approved Network
concepts.body: Network choices are made at design time because they decide whether the job can start. Dataflow workers must reach Google Cloud APIs. When policy forbids external IP addresses, enable Private Google Access on the subnet (or use Private Service Connect for Google APIs) and launch the job with public IPs disabled for its workers; dependencies must then be staged, since workers cannot download packages from the internet. When a central network team owns a Shared VPC, a Dataflow job in a service project runs in a host-project subnet by naming the subnetwork with its full URL, and the launching user needs permission on that subnet. Omitting the network parameters selects the project's default network. Cloud Data Fusion runs its managed resources in a tenant project. A private instance is reached through VPC peering to your VPC, so pipelines can read an on-premises database over Cloud VPN or Interconnect without public endpoints.

concepts.heading: Identity and Encryption per Resource
concepts.body: Every Dataflow job involves two identities. The Dataflow service agent creates and manages resources, while the worker service account is what worker VMs, and therefore the I/O connectors, act as when they read the source and write the sink. By default the worker account is the Compute Engine default service account, which holds broad roles; the docs advise a user-managed service account with the Dataflow Worker role plus minimal data roles at the lowest level, such as editor on one dataset. The launching user needs permission to act as that account. A project Owner launching a job does not give the workers any access to a dataset in another project: grant that dataset to the worker account. Customer-managed encryption keys are also set per resource. Pub/Sub, Dataflow and BigQuery each integrate with Cloud KMS and encrypt their own resources, so a CMEK policy means a key configured on the topic, the job and the table, with key permissions for the service agents and workers.

examPoints: A question that describes plain messages going into a BigQuery table with no transformation and asks for the fewest components points to a BigQuery subscription on the topic, not Dataflow or Dataproc.
A question where Dataflow starts but fails to read or write a dataset despite the launching user being an owner points to the worker service account needing access, not the user.

A question about workers with no external IPs, or a central network team that controls subnets, points to Private Google Access with public IPs disabled, or a Shared VPC subnetwork named by its full URL.

quiz.q: Several teams publish events to one Pub/Sub topic, and downstream subscribers keep failing because some publishers omit required fields. The data lead wants invalid events stopped before any consumer sees them. What should the team do?
choices: Attach an Avro or Protocol Buffer schema to the topic so that non-conforming messages are rejected at publish time
Add a Dataflow job after the topic that drops invalid events and republishes the valid ones to a second topic
Give every subscriber its own validation code and a dead-letter topic for the events that fail validation
Create a BigQuery subscription with a dead-letter table so that invalid events are collected for later review
quiz.explain: A topic schema is a contract enforced when a message is published, so bad data never reaches any subscriber. The Dataflow filter and the per-subscriber checks also catch bad events, but only after the topic accepted them and with more code to run.

quiz.q: A company must replicate an operational PostgreSQL database into Spanner and wants the raw change events kept in Cloud Storage so they can be replayed. Which design fits?
choices: Database Migration Service continuous jobs with Spanner chosen as the destination database for the change events
Datastream writing change events to Cloud Storage, then a Dataflow template that loads the files into Spanner
BigQuery Data Transfer Service scheduled transfers from PostgreSQL into Spanner on a regular nightly cadence
A BigQuery subscription on a Pub/Sub topic that receives the change events and writes them into Spanner
quiz.explain: Datastream captures the changes, Cloud Storage keeps a durable replayable record, and a Dataflow template can load Spanner. Database Migration Service targets Cloud SQL and AlloyDB for PostgreSQL, and the transfer service loads only BigQuery.

recap: Move data with the smallest pipeline: export subscription if nothing changes, Dataflow if it does. Plan contracts, private networking, the worker service account and per-resource CMEK at design time.

title: Streaming I: Pub/Sub Delivery and Dataflow Operations

concepts.heading: Pub/Sub Delivery Features: Dead Letters, Ordering and Exactly-Once
concepts.body: When a subscriber keeps failing on one malformed message, Pub/Sub retries it until the acknowledgment deadline logic gives up. A dead-letter topic fixes this: after a configured number of delivery attempts, between 5 and 100, Pub/Sub forwards the message to the dead-letter topic where another subscription can inspect it. The count is approximate, and it only works when Pub/Sub's service account has the publisher role on the dead-letter topic and the subscriber role on the subscription. Ordering keys deliver messages that share a key in publish order, but only within a region, and a redelivery triggers redelivery of later messages for that key. Exactly-once delivery is enabled per subscription, works within a region, and is supported only on pull subscriptions, including StreamingPull; push and export subscriptions do not support it. Subscribers still must acknowledge within the deadline and avoid repeating work when an acknowledgment fails.

concepts.heading: Replay, Ordering with Dataflow and Regional Failure
concepts.body: Once acknowledged, a message is no longer available to subscribers. Seek changes the acknowledgment state in bulk, either to a snapshot or to a timestamp. A snapshot is a point-in-time view of a subscription's acknowledgment state and lives at most seven days; taking one before a risky deployment is good practice. If a buggy release acknowledged thousands of messages without processing them and no snapshot exists, the recovery route is retention: configure message retention on the topic, or retain acknowledged messages on the subscription, then seek to a time before the deployment. For Dataflow, do not enable message ordering on the subscription: Dataflow groups elements by event timestamp in windows, and the Pub/Sub docs warn that ordering can reduce pipeline performance. For a regional outage, Dataflow lists options by tolerance for loss: wait, run duplicate pipelines in two regions for no loss at the highest cost, or keep two independent subscriptions on the topic, one per region, and start a replacement job on the backup subscription with some potential loss.

concepts.heading: Streaming Engine and Autoscaling
concepts.body: Streaming Engine moves pipeline execution out of the worker VMs into the Dataflow service backend. Workers use less CPU, memory and Persistent Disk, horizontal autoscaling is more responsive and granular, and service updates need no redeployment. It works best with small worker machine types and has a service charge. You cannot switch a running job to Streaming Engine: drain it, then launch it again with the option. Without Streaming Engine, Persistent Disks are allocated at launch, so a later update can raise the worker count only up to the original maximum. With it, state lives in the service and the range can change with an update. For delay-tolerant work such as audit events, a medium or high latency tier makes the autoscaler wait for more backlog before scaling up, saving cost. Autoscaling follows the workers, so a sink limit shows up as more workers with flat throughput: for Bigtable, parallelism comes from cluster nodes, so add nodes.

concepts.heading: Updating, Replacing and Draining a Streaming Job
concepts.body: New pipeline code needs a replacement job. Dataflow runs a compatibility check between the old and new jobs so intermediate state and buffered data can be transferred. If transforms were renamed, supply a transform name mapping linking the new names to the old ones. If the replacement uses a later Beam SDK version, set the update compatibility version to that of the original job. To test validity without launching, add the graph validate only service option and then launch again without it. Drain applies to streaming jobs: the job stops reading, marks sources with an event timestamp at infinity and finishes processing buffered data. Streaming Dataflow retries a failing element indefinitely, so a repeating exception in a parsing step can leave a drain stuck. You can update the draining job with code that fixes the error and the drain completes without data loss; cancelling also works but gives up the buffered data.

examPoints: A question about a poison message that blocks a pull subscriber and must be set aside after a few tries points to a dead-letter topic with a maximum delivery attempts value and the right IAM for the Pub/Sub service account.

A question about reprocessing already acknowledged messages with no snapshot points to topic or subscription retention plus a seek to a timestamp, and about a stuck drain points to updating the draining job with a fix.

A question where more Dataflow workers do not raise throughput and the sink is saturated points to scaling the sink, such as Bigtable nodes, while a delay-tolerant Streaming Engine job points to a higher latency tier.

quiz.q: A pull subscriber keeps failing on one malformed message, and the same message returns again and again. The team wants it set aside after a limited number of attempts so it can be inspected later. What should they configure?
choices: A shorter acknowledgment deadline on the subscription so that the broken message expires sooner and is dropped
A dead-letter topic with a maximum number of delivery attempts, plus the roles the Pub/Sub service account needs on it
Message ordering with an ordering key so that the failing message is skipped and later messages continue
Exactly-once delivery on the subscription so that the failing message is never delivered more than one time
quiz.explain: A dead-letter topic forwards a message after a set number of delivery attempts, and Pub/Sub counts attempts correctly only when its service account holds the publisher and subscriber roles. A shorter deadline just causes faster redelivery, and ordering makes a failing message block later ones for the same key.

quiz.q: A streaming job without Streaming Engine was launched with a maximum of 20 workers. Before a campaign the team updates it to allow 60 workers, but it never scales past 20. What is the reason and the fix?
choices: The autoscaler needs a higher latency tier, so the team should raise the tier and update the running job again
Pub/Sub throttles the subscription, so the team should add more subscriptions and split the topic traffic
Disks were allocated at launch for the original maximum, so relaunch with a higher maximum or use Streaming Engine
The worker service account lacks a role for scaling, so the team should grant it the Dataflow Admin role
quiz.explain: Without Streaming Engine, Persistent Disks are allocated at launch and an update cannot exceed the original maximum, so the job must be relaunched with a higher value or moved to Streaming Engine. A latency tier only tunes how eagerly Streaming Engine jobs scale up.

recap: Dead-letter topics, retention with seek, and one subscription per region cover Pub/Sub failures. Streaming Engine makes scaling flexible; replace jobs with name mappings and fix stuck drains by updating them.

title: Streaming II: Windows, Watermarks, Triggers and Write Semantics

concepts.heading: Windows Group an Unbounded Stream by Event Time
concepts.body: A stream has no end, so aggregations need windows: finite pieces cut by element timestamp. Tumbling windows (Beam calls them fixed) are consistent, disjoint intervals, so each element lands in exactly one window; page views per clock hour is the textbook case. Hopping windows (Beam: sliding) have a fixed length and start every period, so they overlap; a five-minute window starting every minute gives a running average refreshed each minute. Session windows hold elements within a gap duration of each other, and data after the gap starts a new window; they are assigned per key, which suits player activity with a ten-minute gap and sessions of very different lengths. Windows use the element's timestamp. If the pipeline assigns arrival or publish time, a backlog delivered after a six-hour outage lands in the current window and produces a spike. Taking the timestamp from the event's own time field puts delayed events where they belong.

concepts.heading: Watermarks, Late Data and Triggers
concepts.body: A watermark is a threshold for when Dataflow expects all data of a window to have arrived, and the data source determines it. An element with a timestamp inside a window that arrives after the watermark passed the window's end is late data. By default a trigger emits a window's result when the watermark passes its end, and late data is dropped. With the Beam SDK you can set an allowed lateness and add triggers on event time, processing time, element counts or combinations. For hourly order counts where mobile clients deliver orders up to 30 minutes late, allow lateness and add a late trigger so the pipeline emits an on-time result and then refined updates. Data later than the allowed lateness is still dropped. The downstream table must expect updates for a window, because a refined result replaces or supplements the earlier one. Windows that stay open for a long time also keep state per key.

concepts.heading: Exactly-Once, At-Least-Once and BigQuery Write Methods
concepts.body: Dataflow streaming jobs run in exactly-once mode by default: records are not dropped or duplicated as they move through the pipeline. At-least-once mode loses no record but may duplicate some, and it can significantly lower cost and latency. It suits map-only work such as log parsing, per-record schema translation of change data, pipelines that deduplicate downstream, and sinks that cannot guarantee exactly-once. Aggregations like counts and sums, and business-critical uses such as fraud detection, stay exactly-once. Match the BigQuery write method to the mode. STORAGE_WRITE_API gives exactly-once semantics; STORAGE_API_AT_LEAST_ONCE has lower latency but allows duplicate writes. STREAMING_INSERTS is the legacy API, still the default for unbounded collections, with best-effort deduplication, and it is not recommended for new projects. FILE_LOADS is incompatible with at-least-once mode. The Dataflow mode and the connector method should tell the same story.

concepts.heading: Bad Records, Hot Keys and Bounded Sources
concepts.body: Streaming Dataflow retries a failing element indefinitely instead of skipping it, so one bad record can stall a job. Plan a dead-letter path: with the Storage Write API, rows that cannot be written are available as a separate collection from the write result, and parse failures can go to a side output. Route both to a table or bucket with the error and the original payload so the main flow continues and engineers can fix and replay them. Another stall is the hot key. In Streaming Engine the buffered input and state for open windows has a documented limit per key, and exceeding it leaves the pipeline stuck with high system lag. One placeholder ID for all anonymous visitors is the classic cause. Salt the key into shards, aggregate partially and combine in a second step. Finally, a file source run with the streaming flag is still bounded and ends when the files are read. For new files, send bucket notifications to Pub/Sub and read that subscription.

examPoints: A question about a running average that refreshes every minute over five minutes points to hopping (sliding) windows, hourly disjoint totals point to tumbling windows, and activity separated by idle gaps points to session windows.
A question about a spike after a delayed backlog, or orders arriving after the window closed, points to event-time timestamps plus allowed lateness and a late trigger.
A question about duplicates versus cost in a map-only job points to at-least-once mode with STORAGE_API_AT_LEAST_ONCE, while exact counts point to exactly-once with STORAGE_WRITE_API.

quiz.q: A pipeline counts web orders per clock hour by event time. Mobile clients buffer orders offline, so some arrive 30 minutes after the hour ends, and the finished counts are too low. What change addresses this?
choices: Switch to session windows with a thirty-minute gap so that every late order extends the open hourly window
Move to at-least-once mode so that the late orders are delivered again and counted on a second attempt
Replace the event timestamps with the arrival times so that every order falls inside the current window
Allow lateness on the window and add a trigger that emits refined results when late orders arrive
quiz.explain: Allowed lateness keeps the window open for late elements and a late trigger emits updated counts. Arrival time would put orders into the wrong hour, and at-least-once mode concerns duplicates, not lateness.

quiz.q: A map-only streaming job parses application logs and writes them to BigQuery, where a view already removes duplicates. The business wants lower cost and latency and accepts occasional duplicate rows. What fits?
choices: Exactly-once mode with the legacy streaming inserts method, because it deduplicates on a best-effort basis
At-least-once mode with the Storage Write API at-least-once method, accepting duplicates that the view removes
At-least-once mode with the batch file loads method, because load jobs are cheaper for continuous data
Exactly-once mode with a Storage Write API stream per worker so that no duplicate rows can be produced
quiz.explain: A map-only pipeline with downstream deduplication is the case at-least-once mode targets, and the matching connector method is the at-least-once Storage Write API. File loads cannot be combined with that mode, and the legacy inserts are not recommended for new projects.

recap: Pick windows by shape (tumbling, hopping, session), assign event time, and handle late data with allowed lateness and triggers. Match exactly-once or at-least-once to the BigQuery write method, and add dead-letter paths.

title: Batch Processing: Dataproc, Data Fusion, Kafka and Templates

concepts.heading: Dataproc: Separate Storage from Compute
concepts.body: On-premises Hadoop couples storage (HDFS) to the compute nodes, so the cluster must stay up to keep data available. On Google Cloud the usual pattern keeps data in Cloud Storage and treats Dataproc clusters as disposable. The Cloud Storage connector lets Spark and Hive read and write gs:// paths like HDFS, so existing code needs little change. A manufacturer with 300 TB in HDFS and nightly jobs on a cluster idle 18 hours a day copies the data to Cloud Storage, changes paths, and creates a cluster for each run and deletes it afterwards, paying only for the job hours. Dataproc (now branded Managed Service for Apache Spark; the exam guide uses the Dataproc name) offers workflow templates and Cloud Composer operators to create, run and delete clusters automatically. A persistent cluster is justified when many users run interactive work all day.

concepts.heading: Secondary Workers and the BigQuery Connector
concepts.body: A Dataproc cluster has primary workers, which are standard VMs running HDFS DataNodes, and optional secondary workers. Secondary workers only process: they hold no HDFS data, only a local cache. They can be Spot VMs, preemptible VMs or non-preemptible VMs. Because a reclaimed node loses no stored data, Spark can reschedule its tasks, which makes them a cheap way to add peak capacity for fault-tolerant batch jobs. Keep the master and primary workers stable, and keep data in Cloud Storage so even a primary-worker loss is harmless. When a Spark job must read a multi-terabyte BigQuery fact table, use the Spark BigQuery connector. It reads through the BigQuery Storage Read API, which splits the table into streams that executors read in parallel with column projection and filter pushdown, and it writes results back with load jobs or the Storage Write API. A manual export adds a copy, delay and cleanup.

concepts.heading: Cloud Data Fusion and Kafka Integration
concepts.body: Cloud Data Fusion is a managed, code-free integration service built on the open-source CDAP project. Users design pipelines on a canvas by connecting plugins for sources, transforms, aggregates and sinks, and can use Wrangler for interactive cleansing. At run time it provisions an ephemeral Dataproc cluster in your project, runs the pipeline with Spark and deletes the cluster. Choose it when analysts with little programming experience need to pull Oracle tables, join, cleanse and load BigQuery with prebuilt connectors; choose Dataflow or Dataproc when engineers want code-level control. For Apache Kafka in your own data center, Beam's KafkaIO reads topics and Google provides an Apache Kafka to BigQuery Dataflow template, so no pipeline code is needed, but the workers need private connectivity such as Cloud VPN or Interconnect. Teams with Kafka client code that must not change can use Google Cloud Managed Service for Apache Kafka; new workloads without Kafka ties are usually simpler on Pub/Sub.

concepts.heading: Dataflow Templates: Flex Versus Classic
concepts.body: Templates package a pipeline so that design and deployment are separate: a developer builds it, and a permitted user launches it with parameters from the console, gcloud or the REST API, with no Apache Beam SDK or development environment. They are code artifacts that fit source control and CI/CD, and Google provides open source pre-built templates for common cases. A Flex template packages the pipeline as a Docker image in Artifact Registry plus a specification file in Cloud Storage. On launch, the service starts a launcher VM, pulls the image and builds the execution graph from the runtime parameters. That means it needs no ValueProvider, can choose a different I/O connector by parameter and can validate parameters before the job starts; Google recommends it for new templates. A classic template is the serialized static graph, with runtime parameters wrapped in ValueProvider, which not every source and sink supports. Jobs from templates can take several minutes to start.

examPoints: A question about nightly Hadoop or Spark jobs with idle hours and a request for minimal code changes points to data in Cloud Storage with the connector and an ephemeral Dataproc cluster per run.

A question about analysts with little programming experience building batch pipelines points to Cloud Data Fusion, and a question about Kafka events into BigQuery without a custom consumer points to the Dataflow Kafka to BigQuery template.
A question about one reusable template that selects a connector by parameter and validates input before launch points to a Flex template, not a classic template.

quiz.q: A Dataproc cluster runs fault-tolerant nightly Spark jobs, and the team wants cheap extra capacity at the peak without paying for more HDFS storage. What should they add?
choices: Primary workers backed by larger disks, so the cluster gains both extra storage and extra processing power
Secondary workers on Spot VMs, which only process data and hold no HDFS data, so reclaimed nodes lose no stored blocks
A second persistent cluster, so that jobs can be split between the clusters and share the same HDFS blocks
Additional master nodes, so that the scheduler can place more Spark tasks on the existing worker machines
quiz.explain: Secondary workers add compute only, and Spot pricing suits batch work that tolerates reclaimed nodes because Spark reschedules tasks. More primary workers would add HDFS storage the team does not want, and extra masters do not add task capacity.

quiz.q: A team wants one reusable Dataflow template whose pipeline picks a different I/O connector depending on a parameter and validates the parameters before the job starts. Which template type fits?
choices: A classic template with every runtime parameter wrapped in a ValueProvider so that values can be read at launch
A Flex template, because its graph is built at launch from the runtime parameters and can be validated first
A classic template stored in Cloud Storage, because a static graph can switch connectors without a new build
A pre-built Google template, because it accepts an unlimited set of connector choices without any custom code
quiz.explain: A Flex template builds the execution graph dynamically at launch, so it can choose connectors by parameter and validate inputs. A classic template is a fixed serialized graph, and pre-built templates cover only their predefined scenarios.

recap: Keep batch data in Cloud Storage and run ephemeral Dataproc clusters with Spot secondary workers. Use Data Fusion for code-free pipelines, the Kafka template for brokers, and Flex templates for reusable pipelines.

title: BigQuery Transformations, AI Enrichment and Data Acquisition

concepts.heading: Stored Procedures for Reusable SQL Logic
concepts.body: A BigQuery stored procedure is a named, reusable collection of SQL statements saved in a dataset. It accepts IN, OUT and INOUT arguments, can declare variables and use procedural language such as IF, WHILE and RAISE, and callers run it with CALL, including from other datasets they can access. A nightly job that declares a date variable, deletes a partition, inserts recomputed rows, checks the row count and raises an error when it is zero is a natural procedure, and several teams can call the same logic with different arguments. A procedure has no schedule of its own: run it from a scheduled query, Cloud Composer, Workflows or Dataform. SQL procedures execute inside BigQuery; procedures for Apache Spark are a separate type and not what a plain SQL procedure uses. Putting the logic in one place means a fix applies everywhere the procedure is called.

concepts.heading: MERGE for Change Data
concepts.body: BigQuery supports DML, including MERGE, which combines INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE in one statement driven by a join between a source and a target table. It is atomic: all the changes apply or none do. For a nightly staging table that holds a feed of new customers, changed addresses and flagged deletions, one MERGE joins staging to production, uses WHEN MATCHED clauses to update or delete changed keys, and WHEN NOT MATCHED to insert new ones. The alternatives are weaker. Rebuilding the whole table touches every row, separate insert, update and delete statements are not atomic as a group, and appending everything pushes deduplication onto every reader. A MERGE can sit inside a stored procedure, and a single recurring statement with nothing depending on it can run as a BigQuery scheduled query, which is built on BigQuery Data Transfer Service and needs no extra infrastructure.

concepts.heading: Generative AI Enrichment from SQL
concepts.body: BigQuery can call Gemini models from SQL, so unstructured text can be enriched where it already lives. You create a remote model that references a Gemini endpoint through a BigQuery connection, then call AI.GENERATE_TEXT in a query; the scalar AI.GENERATE function can also call Gemini directly without a remote model. Prompt text is built from table columns, inference runs in Google Cloud, and the results are written to a new table. For 5 million support tickets that need a sentiment and a list of topics, this avoids exporting data and needs no labelled training set, because the foundation model follows the prompt. It is plain SQL, so analysts can schedule it. Cost depends on token counts, so test on a sample first. Check current availability of each function in the BigQuery docs before relying on it in a design.

concepts.heading: Extracting Fields from Files and Choosing How Data Arrives
concepts.body: BigQuery can treat objects in Cloud Storage as ObjectRef values, created with OBJ.MAKE_REF from a URI or taken from an object table. Generative AI functions accept them, so a query can send a scanned PDF to Gemini with a prompt. AI.GENERATE with an output schema returns typed fields such as name, date and amount in a STRUCT that can be stored in columns; AI.GENERATE_TABLE is the table-valued variant over a remote model. A table definition over PDFs exposes only metadata or bytes, and regular expressions cannot read scanned images. Acquisition follows the same smallest-tool rule. A BigQuery subscription loads Pub/Sub messages without code, Datastream captures database changes, scheduled queries and the transfer service move recurring loads, and the Storage Write API serves custom streaming writers. Pick the entry point from the source type and whether any transformation happens on the way.

examPoints: A question about reusable multi-step SQL logic with variables and error handling shared by several teams points to a BigQuery stored procedure called with CALL, scheduled from outside.
A question about applying inserts, updates and deletes from a staging table atomically points to a MERGE statement with WHEN MATCHED and WHEN NOT MATCHED clauses.
A question about labelling millions of rows or extracting fields from PDFs without moving data points to BigQuery remote models and AI.GENERATE functions, with ObjectRef values for files.

quiz.q: Each night a staging table receives new customers, changed addresses and flagged deletions. The engineer must apply all of it to the production table so that either everything is applied or nothing is. What should the engineer use?
choices: Three separate statements run in order: first an INSERT, then an UPDATE and finally a DELETE statement
A scheduled query that rebuilds the whole production table from staging by using CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE
A MERGE statement that joins staging to production, with WHEN MATCHED and WHEN NOT MATCHED clauses
An append-only load of the staging rows into production, with a view that picks the latest row per key
quiz.explain: MERGE applies inserts, updates and deletes from one join in a single atomic statement. Separate statements are not atomic as a group, a rebuild rewrites every row, and append-only pushes deduplication onto each reader.

quiz.q: A claims team has 200,000 scanned PDF forms in Cloud Storage and needs the claimant name, date and amount as typed BigQuery columns, without exporting the files. Which approach fits?
choices: Define an external table over the bucket and parse the PDF content with regular expressions in SQL
Load the PDFs into Bigtable and let the table parse each form into columns using its built-in parser
Reference the files as ObjectRef values and call AI.GENERATE with an output schema to return typed fields
Run a daily scheduled query that copies the PDF metadata into a table and splits the file names
quiz.explain: ObjectRef values let a query send each document to Gemini, and an output schema returns typed fields that can be stored. An external table exposes only metadata or raw bytes, and regular expressions cannot read scanned images.

recap: Reusable SQL goes in stored procedures, atomic change data in MERGE, simple schedules in scheduled queries. Enrich text and files with Gemini from SQL, and pick the entry point from the source and the transformation.

title: Deployment and Operation: Cloud Composer, Workflows and CI/CD

concepts.heading: Match the Orchestrator to the Complexity
concepts.body: Scheduling choices form a ladder, and operations effort and idle cost grow with each rung. A single recurring SQL statement fits a BigQuery scheduled query. A few dependent SQL steps fit Dataform workflow configurations or a stored procedure called by a scheduled query. Calls across services without Airflow needs fit Workflows, triggered by Cloud Scheduler. Many dependent tasks across services with retries and backfills fit Cloud Composer. Workflows is a serverless orchestrator: steps in YAML or JSON call HTTP endpoints and Google Cloud connectors, branch, loop, retry, wait for callbacks and keep state, billed per step with no cost while idle. Cloud Composer (now Managed Service for Apache Airflow; the exam guide uses Cloud Composer) runs DAGs with a large operator library, schedules and backfills on an environment with a baseline cost. Existing Airflow code or dozens of dependent tasks favor Composer; light API glue favors Workflows.

concepts.heading: Workflows: Connectors and Retries
concepts.body: A connector is a built-in wrapper around a Google Cloud API such as BigQuery, Dataflow, Cloud Run or Dataproc. Compared with a raw HTTP call it handles authentication with the workflow's service account, applies retry behavior for transient errors and, for long-running operations, waits for completion, so the author writes no polling loop or job-ID handling. Use http.get or http.post only for APIs without a connector, such as third-party services, and add your own retry and wait logic. For a flaky external API that occasionally returns 503, wrap the call in a try step with a retry policy: a predicate for transient errors, such as the built-in http.default_retry covering 429, 502, 503 and 504, a maximum number of attempts and an exponential backoff. Backoff gives the service time to recover and avoids retry storms. Moving to Composer does not remove the need to define retries.

concepts.heading: Composer Operations: Sensors, Triggers, Cleanup and Secrets
concepts.body: A sensor is an Airflow task that waits for a condition such as a file in Cloud Storage. In the default poke mode it holds a worker slot for the whole wait, so many sensors on a busy morning can starve other tasks. A deferrable sensor hands the wait to the triggerer, an asynchronous component, so the task frees its slot until the condition is met; the environment must run at least one triggerer. Reschedule mode also frees the slot between checks. For events, a Cloud Storage object finalize event can invoke a Cloud Run function that calls the environment's Airflow REST API to start a DAG run, passing the file name in the run's conf. Cleanup tasks need the all_done trigger rule: the default all_success skips the delete-cluster task when the Spark job fails and leaves a Dataproc cluster running. Move passwords and keys out of source control by configuring Secret Manager as the Airflow secrets backend.

concepts.heading: CI/CD for Pipelines
concepts.body: Treat pipeline code like application code: Git, review, automated tests and a repeatable release. A Composer environment reads DAGs from the dags folder of a Cloud Storage bucket it owns. A sound flow runs DAG-integrity (import) tests and unit tests of custom operators in a build service such as Cloud Build when a pull request opens, then copies reviewed files into the production environment's dags folder after merge. Editing production files directly bypasses review. For Dataform, a release configuration compiles a chosen Git branch or tag into a compilation result, and a workflow configuration executes it on a cron schedule with a chosen service account, so only reviewed code on the production branch runs each morning. For Dataflow Flex Templates, Cloud Build runs tests, builds the container image into Artifact Registry with a version tag, and creates the specification file in Cloud Storage. Other projects then launch from the spec, and versioned images give rollback.

examPoints: A question about chaining HTTP calls and connectors, waiting for a callback and paying nothing while idle points to Workflows, while backfills, existing Airflow DAGs or dozens of dependent data tasks point to Cloud Composer.
A question about DAG sensors starving worker slots points to deferrable sensors, and a cleanup task skipped after a failure points to the all_done trigger rule.

A question about production runs from reviewed code points to CI with Cloud Build, a Dataform release plus workflow configuration, or a Flex Template image in Artifact Registry with a spec in Cloud Storage.

quiz.q: A finance analyst needs a single MERGE statement to run every night at 02:00. Nothing depends on it and no other tasks need coordination. Which option fits best?
choices: A Cloud Composer environment with a DAG that runs the statement on a nightly schedule at 02:00
A BigQuery scheduled query that runs the statement on a schedule, with no infrastructure to maintain
A Workflows definition triggered by Cloud Scheduler that calls the BigQuery API with the statement
A Dataproc workflow template that starts a cluster, runs the statement through Spark and then deletes it
quiz.explain: One recurring statement belongs on the lowest rung of the ladder: a scheduled query needs nothing else. Composer and Workflows can run it, but they add an environment or definition to maintain for no benefit, and Dataproc is unrelated to a SQL statement.

quiz.q: A DAG creates a Dataproc cluster, runs a Spark job and deletes the cluster. When the job fails, the delete task is skipped and the cluster keeps running. What is the best fix?
choices: Increase the retries on the Spark job task so that the failing job eventually succeeds and the DAG continues
Set the delete task's trigger rule to all_done so that it runs whether the job task succeeded or failed
Run a weekly cleanup DAG that lists and deletes any cluster created by the pipeline in the past week
Switch the sensor tasks to deferrable mode so that the failed job releases its worker slot and the cluster
quiz.explain: The default all_success rule skips a task whose upstream failed, whereas all_done runs it after upstream tasks finish in any state. More retries hide real bugs, and a weekly sweep still leaves up to a week of cost.

recap: Use the lowest rung that fits: scheduled query, Dataform, Workflows, then Composer. Free worker slots with deferrable sensors, clean up with all_done, keep secrets in Secret Manager, and release through CI.
